strengths: Addresses a novel and practically important problem: post-training quantization of large-scale 3D reconstruction transformers (VGGT), which is unexplored prior to this work.

Provides clear empirical motivation via visualization of heavy-tailed distributions caused by data-independent special tokens (camera/register tokens) and calibration instability from multi-view redundancy.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple bit-widths (W8A8, W6A6, W4A4), two different 3D tasks (camera pose estimation on Co3Dv2, point map estimation on DTU), and multiple frame counts, showing consistent improvements over strong baselines (GPTQ, SmoothQuant, QuaRot, DopQ-ViT).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of rotation vs. scaling, quantization granularity, and each component of the sampling strategy (filtering vs. clustering), with variance reported across random seeds.
Real hardware latency/memory measurements demonstrate practical speedups (2.5x) and compression (3.7x) with minimal additional overhead from the proposed smoothing and calibration techniques.
Good reproducibility details (hyperparameters, calibration set size, learning rates) and promise of code release.
weaknesses: The core technical contributions are largely a combination/adaptation of existing techniques (Hadamard rotation from QuaRot/QuIP#, channel-wise smoothing similar to SmoothQuant/AWQ-style approaches, deep-layer statistics-based outlier filtering, and clustering-based calibration sampling) rather than fundamentally new algorithmic ideas; novelty is primarily in the application domain and specific combination.

Theorem 3.2 rests on a fairly restrictive assumption (that sub-region scales are equal across domains, V*_j = V*_i for all i,j) that trivializes the problem into a basic maximum-entropy/uniform-sampling argument; the theoretical justification is somewhat superficial relative to how it is framed as a central contribution.

Evaluation is limited to a single base model (VGGT-1B) and only two datasets/tasks (Co3Dv2, DTU); no evaluation on other emerging 3D reconstruction transformers (e.g., Fast3R, DUSt3R-family) to demonstrate generality of the proposed quantization framework beyond VGGT.

Despite headline claims of '98% of full-precision performance,' this holds mainly for the least-sensitive metric (AUC@30); more stringent metrics (AUC@3) show substantially larger relative degradation (e.g., 43.6 vs. 54.9, ~20% relative drop) at W4A4, suggesting the abstract's characterization may overstate the robustness of the approach at the most aggressive bit-width.

No comparison with quantization-aware training (QAT) approaches or discussion of the performance ceiling achievable with more expensive calibration/fine-tuning, which would help contextualize how much headroom remains.

Baseline methods (GPTQ, SmoothQuant, QuaRot) are generic techniques not specifically adapted to the VGGT architecture, so the comparison, while informative, may not represent the strongest possible baseline tuning effort, potentially inflating the apparent margin of improvement.

Limited discussion of failure cases, sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., cluster count K, filtering threshold T), or scenarios where the proposed method might not generalize (e.g., very different scene types or extreme frame counts).

strengths: First systematic PTQ framework tailored to VGGT-style 3D reconstruction transformers, addressing a clear and practical deployment need (billion-scale 3D models are compute/memory heavy).

Well-motivated technical contributions grounded in empirical observations specific to VGGT: (1) heavy-tailed activations caused by data-independent camera/register tokens, and (2) calibration instability from the multi-view, redundant nature of 3D data.

Dual-Smoothed Fine-Grained Quantization (pre-Hadamard rotation + post-local channel smoothing computed in rotated space) is a sensible, largely training/inference-cost-free adaptation that empirically reduces quantization error substantially (Table 4 ablation).

Noise-Filtered Diverse Sampling leverages a reasonable structural prior (first-frame vs. subsequent-frame correlation) for calibration clustering, supported by a maximum-entropy argument (Theorem 3.2) and validated with variance-reduction experiments (Fig. 5, Fig. 8).

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple tasks (camera pose estimation, point map estimation, point cloud reconstruction) and datasets (CO3Dv2, DTU, 7-Scenes, NRGBD), with consistent, often large improvements over strong baselines (QuaRot, SmoothQuant, AWQ, GPTQ, RepQ-ViT, DopQ-ViT) especially at aggressive W4A4 settings.
Real hardware profiling (CUTLASS on RTX 4090) demonstrating actual 2.5x latency reduction and 3.7x memory reduction, not just theoretical FLOPs savings.

Reasonably thorough ablations in the appendix: hyperparameter sensitivity (α, Hadamard seed, filter threshold p, cluster number K, sample size), quantization granularity trade-offs, calibration compute overhead, and cross-architecture generalization test on Fast3R.
Comparison to an orthogonal acceleration method (FastVGGT) situates the contribution well within the broader efficient-3D-reconstruction landscape.
Clear reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, promised code release, proof of theorem, and visual qualitative comparisons.
weaknesses: Core techniques (Hadamard rotation, activation-weight smoothing, K-Means-based calibration clustering) are adaptations/combinations of existing PTQ methods (QuaRot, SmoothQuant, GPTQ-style calibration) rather than fundamentally new quantization mechanisms; novelty is primarily in domain-specific application and combination rather than new algorithmic principles.

Theorem 3.2 relies on strong idealizing assumptions (uniform sub-region scales V*_j = V*/N*) and essentially reduces to a maximum-entropy argument; its practical link to the proposed frame-aware clustering heuristic is loosely justified rather than rigorously derived.

Reported headline claim of '>98% of full-precision performance' appears to hold mainly for looser metrics (e.g., AUC@30); under stricter metrics (AUC@3), the gap is much larger (e.g., 43.6 vs. 54.9, only ~79%), suggesting the abstract's framing may overstate the method's fidelity at W4A4.

Generalization beyond VGGT is tested on only one additional architecture (Fast3R), limiting confidence that the proposed frame-aware clustering (which exploits VGGT's specific first-frame-centric inductive bias) generalizes broadly to other 3D transformer designs without similar architecture.

The fixed choice of α=0.5 for the scaling factor, while shown to be relatively robust in a narrow sensitivity sweep (0.3–0.7), is not deeply analyzed for its interaction with the rotation step across varied layer types.

No explicit limitations section discussing where the method still underperforms (e.g., tight-threshold pose accuracy at 4-bit, or scenarios with atypical first-frame statistics beyond the constructed extreme-case test).

Comparisons omit possibly relevant recent quantization methods tailored to multi-view or geometric transformers (if any exist), and the baseline set, while reasonably broad, is drawn mostly from LLM/ViT quantization literature adapted post hoc.
